Block overview

How this block develops

Block 4 ended with REINFORCE using a learned prompt-only baseline. Its final question was: What happens when the reward being maximised is a learned scorer? We start with that question. A higher score can fail to mean a better response, so we first change the objective and then examine two ways to train the generator.

Learning scope and preparation

This narrative accompanies the Block 5 microlectures. Before you start, review response probabilities, the score-function identity and REINFORCE with a learned prompt-only baseline from Block 4.

Classroom core: reference-policy KL regularisation, the conceptual PPO update, and DPO through Bradley–Terry. Required assessed reading: no new reading assignment is issued in this narrative. Coding assignment: no new coding assignment is issued here. Optional enrichment: detailed optimisation proofs, TRPO, actor–critic methods, bootstrapping and GAE. Self-check and discussion questions are for practice. Listing a source does not make it assessed reading.

Microlecture 1

RLHF with a reference policy

Instructor: Video · Slides (PDF)

AI version: Video · Slides (PDF)

From expected reward to a regularised objective

Block 4 maximised the expected score of a frozen reward model for each prompt:

Jx(θ)=𝔼o∼πθ(·|x)[rϕ(x,o)]

This is the objective in J&M Eq. 8.5. Block 4 maximised it by REINFORCE with a learned prompt-only baseline (Sutton and Barto §§13.3–13.4). Block 4 closed with a question: what happens when the reward being maximised is a learned scorer? A higher learned score can fail to mean a better response. This microlecture changes the objective to account for that, and then checks how the REINFORCE update changes.

Problems and solutions in this microlecture
ProblemSolution
A learned scorer can rate an unfaithful response highly, so maximising its score can reward the scorer’s errors.Keep a frozen SFT reference
Limiting departure from πref needs one number that compares two response distributions.KL divergence
The adjusted reward depends on θ. We must check its gradient.Adjust the reward

Can a higher learned score fail to mean a better response?

When the learned score rewards an error

The reward model was trained on a limited set of preference comparisons. It predicts which response people would prefer. It does not observe every response that the generator can produce. Optimising its score can therefore favour errors in the scorer.

A failure of the learned score

Prompt: Summarise this in one sentence: “The launch moved from Monday to Friday.”

Candidate responseLearned scoreCheck against the source
“The launch was postponed from Monday to Friday.”2Preserves the stated information.
“The launch was successfully completed on Friday.”5Adds a claim that the source does not support.

Suppose the scorer has learned to favour confident reports of success. Raising the probability of the second response raises expected learned reward and lowers faithfulness to the source.

This is reward exploitation: the policy finds responses that score well under the learned objective and fail the intended human goal. J&M §8.4 gives a second reason for restraint. The policy starts from a capable SFT model, and the preference data are small. Moving far from the SFT policy can change useful behaviours that the preference data do not measure.

What starting behaviour should the policy retain while it learns from preferences?

The frozen SFT reference

Keep a frozen copy of the supervised fine-tuned model. Call its response distribution the reference policy, πref. The trainable policy, πθ, starts from the same model. The reference stays fixed during this RLHF stage.

The reference gives a distribution over completed responses for each prompt. It is a starting point. It does not give a target answer for each prompt. A response that was unlikely under the reference needs enough reward to justify a large increase in its probability.

The reference can itself make errors, so staying close to it does not establish truth or usefulness. The intended trade-off is to gain reward while limiting departure from the starting behaviour. The penalty limits departure from the reference. Reward-model errors can remain.

Two copies of the SFT model
CopyRoleDuring RLHF
πθ ← πSFTTrainable generatorUpdated by the policy-gradient steps
πref ← πSFTStarting distribution for the penaltyFrozen

How can we measure departure between two response distributions?

KL divergence from the reference

Fix a prompt x. Compare the current and reference probability of each completed response through their log-ratio, ℓθ(x, o) = ln [πθ(o | x) / πref(o | x)]. The log-ratio is positive when the current policy assigns the response more probability, and negative when it assigns less. Average it using the current policy’s response probabilities:

DKL(πθ∥πref)=∑oπθ(o|x)ln⁡πθ(o|x)πref(o|x)=𝔼o∼πθ[ℓθ(x,o)]

This is the Kullback–Leibler divergence, with direction current policy to reference policy. It is nonnegative, and it is zero when the two distributions agree. It is not symmetric. We assume that the reference gives positive probability wherever the current policy does.

Both policies generate a response token by token, so each response probability is a product of token probabilities, including EOS, as in Block 4. The log-ratio of a response is therefore a sum of token log-ratios:

ℓθ(x,o)=ln⁡πθ(o|x)πref(o|x)=∑tln⁡πθ(ot|x,o<t)πref(ot|x,o<t)

Evaluating ℓθ for a sampled response needs one forward pass of each model over the same tokens. The reference scores the tokens. It does not generate them.

The cat example

Return to Complete: The cat. Let p = πθ(sat . EOS | x). The rewards are 2 for sat . EOS and −1 for flew . EOS, and the reference probability of sat . EOS is 0.75. Take a current policy with p = 0.90.

The log-ratios are ln(0.90/0.75) = 0.1823 for sat . EOS and ln(0.10/0.25) = −0.9163 for flew . EOS. Weighting them by the current probabilities gives

DKL = 0.90 × 0.1823 + 0.10 × (−0.9163) = 0.0725 nats.

If one response has a negative log-ratio, does that make the KL negative?

No. Each response contributes its current probability times its log-ratio. The full sum is nonnegative, even though some terms can be negative. Here the −0.9163 term carries weight 0.10.

How should the training objective trade learned reward against this departure?

The regularised reward objective

Subtract a KL penalty from expected learned reward. The coefficient β > 0 sets the strength of the penalty:

Jβ(θ)=𝔼x∼D[𝔼o∼πθ[rϕ(x,o)]−βDKL(πθ∥πref)]

This is J&M Eqs. 8.6–8.7, with the prompt average written explicitly. The reward-model parameters ϕ and the reference stay fixed. A larger β penalises the same departure more strongly. Its effect depends on the scale of the rewards. Here β is the regularisation coefficient; Block 4 used the same symbol for the baseline learning rate, which we now write as αb.

Because the KL is itself an expectation under πθ, both terms combine into one expectation of an adjusted reward:

Rθ(x,o)=rϕ(x,o)−βℓθ(x,o),Jβ(θ)=𝔼x,o[Rθ(x,o)]

J&M Eq. 8.7 writes the objective in this form. The adjusted reward depends on θ through its log-ratio. The baseline in Block 4 left the expected gradient unchanged. This penalty deliberately changes the objective.

The reward–departure trade-off in the cat example

With p = πθ(sat . EOS | x), rewards 2 and −1, and reference probability 0.75, the expected reward is 3p − 1. For β = 2:

Fixed reference probability 0.75; natural logarithms
Current pExpected rewardKLReward − 2 KL
0.751.25000.00001.2500
0.901.70000.07251.5551
0.991.97000.24271.4847

Moving from 0.75 to 0.90 improves the regularised objective. Moving further to 0.99 increases raw reward, and its added KL cost leaves a lower regularised objective than at 0.90. Computed numerically, the maximum over p is at p = 0.931, where the objective is 1.568. Without the penalty, expected reward keeps rising up to p = 1.

If β increases, must the policy return exactly to the reference?

No. A larger β makes departure more costly, so the maximum moves closer to 0.75. For finite β, a reward gain can still justify some change.

How the reference limits a scorer error

Return to the launch summary. Let A be the faithful response and B the response that adds an unsupported claim. The scorer overrates B: rϕ(x, B) − rϕ(x, A) = 5 − 2 = 3. For a fixed reward, the policy that maximises the regularised objective has a simple form, derived in ML03:

odds of B to A under the optimum = odds of B to A under πref × exp[(rB − rA)/β].

Two consequences follow.

  • The scorer can only reweight what the SFT model already does. A reward error of size δ multiplies the odds by exp(δ/β), a finite factor. Without the penalty, the maximiser puts all its probability on whichever response the scorer rates highest, so a single scoring error takes the whole distribution.
  • A response that the SFT model rarely produces stays rare unless its reward gap is large. Raising a response from reference probability 0.001 to even odds with one at 0.5 needs a gap of β ln 500, about 12.4 reward units at β = 2.
Optimal probability of B, two responses, reward gap 3 in favour of B
πref(B)β = 1β = 2β = 5No penalty
0.10.6910.3320.1681
0.010.1690.0430.0181
0.0010.0200.0040.0021

Keeping the policy near its starting distribution can reduce exposure to scorer errors on unfamiliar responses. It does not guarantee scorer reliability. Preference data can come from several models or other sources (J&M §8.3.1).

The penalty does not correct the scorer. In the first row, B still rises from 0.1 to 0.332 at β = 2. Only a better scorer or better preference data removes the error.

The SFT model gives B probability 0.01 and the scorer overrates it by 3. With β = 2, what probability does the optimum give B?

The odds of B to A are 0.01/0.99 under the reference. Multiplying by exp(3/2) = 4.48 gives odds 0.0453, so the probability is 0.0453/1.0453 = 0.043. Without the penalty it would be 1.

The penalty depends on θ. How does the REINFORCE update change?

The gradient with a KL penalty

Differentiate Jβ. The reward model and the reference stay fixed. The adjusted reward depends on θ, so the policy appears twice: in the sampling distribution and in the log-ratio. Differentiating both gives

∇θJβ=𝔼x,o[Rθ(x,o)∇θln⁡πθ(o|x)]−β𝔼x,o[∇θln⁡πθ(o|x)]

The second expectation is zero. It is the identity behind the Block 4 baseline:

𝔼o∼πθ[∇θln⁡πθ(o|x)]=∑o∇θπθ(o|x)=∇θ1=0

So the score-function identity still applies. REINFORCE uses the adjusted reward Rθ in place of rϕ. Treat Rθ as a constant during backpropagation. Differentiating through both the sampled weight and its log-probability factor would give a different estimator.

Adjusted rewards in the cat example

Take p = 0.90 and β = 2.

sat . EOS: ℓθ = 0.1823, so Rθ = 2 − 2 × 0.1823 = 1.6354.

flew . EOS: ℓθ = −0.9163, so Rθ = −1 − 2 × (−0.9163) = 0.8326.

The penalty lowers the adjusted reward of a response whose probability has risen above the reference, and raises it for one whose probability has fallen. Their current-policy mean, 0.90 × 1.6354 + 0.10 × 0.8326 = 1.5551, is the regularised objective in the table above.

With the Block 4 parameterisation p = σ(z), the exact slope of expected reward at p = 0.90 is dJx/dz = 3p(1 − p) = 0.2700. The exact slope of the regularised objective is dJβ/dz = 0.0722. The penalty slows the push towards sat . EOS.

At πθ = πref, every log-ratio is zero, so the KL contribution to the gradient is zero. The penalty starts to act once the policy moves.

How do sampling, the reference model and the adjusted reward combine in one training loop?

RLHF with a KL penalty

The Block 4 algorithm needs two changes: score each sampled response with the reference as well as the reward model, and use the adjusted reward in place of the learned reward.

  1. Initialise. πθ ← πSFT and πref ← πSFT, with πref frozen. The reward model rϕ from Block 3 is frozen.
  2. Sample a batch. xi ∼ D and oi ∼ πθ(· | xi), for i = 1, …, N.
  3. Score. ri = rϕ(xi, oi) and ℓi = ∑t [ln πθ(oi,t | xi, oi,<t) − ln πref(oi,t | xi, oi,<t)]. Sums run over response tokens. Include EOS. Exclude prompt and padding tokens.
  4. Adjust and centre. Ri = ri − β ℓi and Ai = Ri − bψ(xi). Treat the advantages as constants during the policy update.
  5. Update the policy. Minimise Lπ = −(1/N) ∑i Ai ∑t ln πθ(oi,t | xi, oi,<t) with one step θ ← θ − α ∇θ Lπ.
  6. Fit the baseline. Minimise Lb = (1/N) ∑i (bψ(xi) − Ri)2 with ψ ← ψ − αb ∇ψ Lb. The baseline now estimates the expected adjusted reward.
  7. Repeat. Draw a fresh batch from the updated policy.

Each batch costs generation, one reward-model call per response, and a forward pass of the reference. It then supports one policy update and is discarded.

Generating responses is expensive. Can we make several updates using one sampled batch?

Check your understanding

Quick questions · 3 MCQs and 2 MSQs

An MSQ is correct only when you select all correct options and no extras. Scores are for self-checking. You can revisit a question and change your selection.

Self-study questions
  1. Compute the KL divergence and the regularised objective with β = 2 at p = 0.60. Explain why the objective is lower than at the reference.
  2. Compute DKL(πref ∥ πθ) at p = 0.90 and compare it with 0.0725. What does the comparison show?
  3. Show that the maximum of the regularised objective moves towards 0.75 as β increases, by evaluating it at p = 0.85 and 0.95 for β = 2 and β = 5.
  4. In the summarisation example, could the KL penalty alone stop the policy from favouring the unsupported response? What else would be needed?
  5. Why is the baseline fitted to the adjusted rewards Ri and not to the learned rewards ri?

Microlecture recap

IdeaWhat to retain
Learned-reward failureA limited learned scorer can rate an unfaithful response highly. Maximising it can reward the scorer’s errors.
Reference policyA frozen copy of the SFT model, πref. The trainable policy starts from the same model.
KL divergenceThe current-policy average of response log-ratios. Nonnegative, zero when the policies agree, not symmetric. Example: 0.0725 nats at p = 0.90.
Regularised objectiveJβ = expected learned reward − β KL (J&M Eqs. 8.6–8.7). With β = 2 the example maximum is at p = 0.931.
GradientREINFORCE with the adjusted reward Rθ = rϕ − β ℓθ, held constant during backpropagation.
LimitationThe penalty limits departure from the reference. Reward-model errors can remain.

Microlecture 2

PPO and updates from a sampled batch

Instructor: Video · Slides (PDF)

AI version: Video · Slides (PDF)

J&M §8.4.1 (PPO) is marked TBD in the supplied draft. This microlecture follows Lambert (2026), Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, Ch. 6, and Sutton and Barto §5.5 for importance sampling. Schulman et al. (2017) is the original PPO paper.

From one update per batch to several

ML01 ended with REINFORCE on the KL-adjusted reward. Each batch is sampled from the current policy, scored, and used for one gradient step. After that step the policy has changed, so the batch no longer comes from it and is discarded:

Lπ=−1N∑iAi∑tln⁡πθ(oi,t|xi,oi,<t),Ai=Ri−bψ(xi)

Generation and reward-model scoring dominate the cost of this loop. PPO, proximal policy optimisation, makes several updates from each batch. Doing so raises three problems.

Problems and solutions in this microlecture
ProblemSolution
Each batch gives one update and is discarded. Generating responses is expensive.Reuse the batch
After one update, the stored responses no longer come from the current policy, so the REINFORCE estimate no longer applies.Reweight by the probability ratio
Repeated updates move the policy away from πold, where the surrogate is no longer accurate.Clip the ratio

What has to be stored if one batch is to support several updates?

Reusing a rollout batch

Store the policy that generated the batch as πold, the rollout policy. In practice we store its token log-probabilities for the sampled responses. Keep these and the advantage estimates fixed while optimising on the batch. After this optimisation stage, copy the current policy into πold and collect a fresh batch.

Three copies of the policy now play different roles. The table orders them by how often they change.

Policy copies during RLHF with PPO
PolicyRoleWhen it changes
πrefAnchors the KL penalty to the SFT model (ML01)Never, during this RLHF stage
πoldGenerated the current batchBetween batches
πθTrainable generatorAt every gradient step

At the start of RLHF, all three are copies of the SFT model: πref = πold = πθ = πSFT. The rollout policy is set just before each batch is generated, by copying πold ← πθ. For the first batch no update has happened, so πold = πref. For each later batch, πold is πθ as it stands after the previous batch's gradient steps. Lambert (Ch. 6) notes that one to four gradient steps per batch is common; the ratio defined below is exactly 1 on the first step of each batch.

After the first gradient step, πθ differs from πold. The stored responses were drawn from πold, so treating them as fresh samples from πθ gives a biased gradient estimate. Regenerating would give a different batch in any case, because sampling is random. What changes when πθ moves is the distribution the responses come from.

What goes wrong if we reuse the cat batch after one update?

Reusing the cat batch

Take the first batch of RLHF for Complete: The cat, so πold = πref, with πold(sat . EOS | x) = 0.75. Every log-ratio to the reference is zero, so the adjusted rewards equal the learned rewards: 2 for sat . EOS and −1 for flew . EOS.

Step 1. Baseline and advantages

The baseline is the expected adjusted reward under πold for this prompt:

b = 0.75 × 2 + 0.25 × (−1) = 1.25.

Subtract it from each reward:

sat: Â = 2 − 1.25 = 0.75.    flew: Â = −1 − 1.25 = −2.25.

sat is common and slightly above average. flew is rare and far below it, so its advantage is large and negative. Weighted by how often πold produces each response, the advantages average to zero: 0.75 × 0.75 + 0.25 × (−2.25) = 0.5625 − 0.5625 = 0. Here the baseline is the exact expected reward; a learned baseline bψ (ML01, step 6) converges to it.

Step 2. The stored batch and one update

The stored batch is sat, sat, sat, flew: proportions 3 : 1, as πold produces. Now take one update that moves p = πθ(sat . EOS | x) to 0.80. A fresh batch from πθ would have proportions 4 : 1 on average, and its expected reward is 3p − 1 = 1.40.

Step 3. Mean reward from the stored batch, reused unchanged

¼[3 × 2 + 1 × (−1)] = 1.25.

Mean reward of the stored batch
FactorValueWhere it comes from
¼¼Average over the four stored responses
3 × 26Three sat responses, reward 2 each
1 × (−1)−1One flew, reward −1
Result1.25The exact value at p = 0.80 is 1.40

Step 4. Gradient estimate from the ML01 loss, reused unchanged

Treat p as the parameter. The ML01 estimate averages, over the batch, each response's advantage times the derivative of its own log-probability:

1N∑iA^iddpln⁡π(oi)

For sat, ln π(sat) = ln p, so the derivative is 1/p. For flew, ln π(flew) = ln(1 − p), so the derivative is −1/(1 − p). With N = 4:

¼[3 × 0.75 × (1/p) + 1 × (−2.25) × (−1/(1 − p))] = ¼[2.25/p + 2.25/(1 − p)].

Gradient estimate from the stored batch
FactorWhere it comes from
¼Average over the four stored responses
3Three stored sat responses
0.75Advantage of sat (step 1)
1/pDerivative of ln p, the log-probability of sat
1One stored flew
−2.25Advantage of flew (step 1)
−1/(1 − p)Derivative of ln(1 − p), the log-probability of flew; its minus sign cancels the minus sign of the advantage

At p = 0.80: 2.25/0.80 = 2.8125 and 2.25/0.20 = 11.25, so the estimate is ¼(14.0625) = 3.52. The exact slope of the expected reward 3p − 1 is 3.

At p = 0.75 the same expression gives 2.25/0.75 = 3 and 2.25/0.25 = 9, so ¼(3 + 9) = 3 exactly. Before the update the estimate is right. After it, the stored batch keeps the proportions 3 : 1, so it cannot see the update, and the estimate is biased. At p = 0.90 it is 6.25: the error grows as πθ moves away from πold.

Why does the stored batch give the right slope at p = 0.75 but not at 0.80?

At 0.75 the batch proportions 3 : 1 match the current policy, so averaging over the batch is averaging under πθ. At 0.80 the current policy produces 4 : 1, but the batch still has 3 : 1. The estimate gives flew too much weight relative to πθ, and its large term 2.25/(1 − p) inflates the result.

How can the stored batch report what the current policy would produce?

Reweighting the cat batch

Weight each stored response by the ratio of its current probability to its rollout probability. At p = 0.80:

sat: 0.80/0.75 = 1.067.    flew: 0.20/0.25 = 0.8.

The weighted counts are 3 × 1.067 = 3.2 for sat and 0.8 for flew. That is 4 : 1, the proportions of the current policy, recovered without generating again.

Step 5. Reweighted mean reward

Each response now counts as its weight times its reward:

¼[3 × 1.067 × 2 + 1 × 0.8 × (−1)] = ¼[6.4 − 0.8] = 1.40.

Reweighted mean reward
FactorValueWhere it comes from
¼¼Average over the four stored responses
3 × 1.067 × 26.4Three sat, weight 0.80/0.75, reward 2
1 × 0.8 × (−1)−0.8One flew, weight 0.20/0.25, reward −1
Result1.40The exact value 3p − 1 at p = 0.80

Step 6. The ratio surrogate, with p free

Now keep p free and use the advantages in place of the rewards. Each term is count × ratio × advantage:

¼[3 × (p/0.75) × 0.75 + 1 × ((1 − p)/0.25) × (−2.25)].

Ratio surrogate for the stored batch
FactorWhere it comes from
¼Average over the four stored responses
3Three stored sat responses
p/0.75Ratio for sat: current probability p over rollout probability 0.75
0.75Advantage of sat
1One stored flew
(1 − p)/0.25Ratio for flew: current probability 1 − p over rollout probability 0.25
−2.25Advantage of flew

Simplify term by term. 3 × (p/0.75) × 0.75 = 3p. ((1 − p)/0.25) × (−2.25) = −9(1 − p) = −9 + 9p. So the surrogate is ¼(3p − 9 + 9p) = ¼(12p − 9) = 3p − 2.25.

The surrogate predicts the gain of the current policy over πold: 0 at p = 0.75, and 0.15 at p = 0.80, which is 1.40 − 1.25. Using advantages in place of rewards subtracts the constant 1.25: the slope is unchanged, and the surrogate is zero at πold. The adjusted rewards stay frozen for the batch, so the KL penalty is re-evaluated only at the next batch. With β = 2 the regularised objective of ML01 gains 0.31 at p = 0.90, against the 0.45 that the surrogate predicts, because the KL penalty grows as p moves.

Step 7. The reweighted gradient

Differentiate each term. The derivative of a ratio is the ratio times the derivative of the log-probability:

¼[3 × 0.75 × (p/0.75) × (1/p) + 1 × (−2.25) × ((1 − p)/0.25) × (−1/(1 − p))] = ¼[3 + 9] = 3.

For sat, the p in the ratio cancels the 1/p, so each copy contributes 0.75 × (1/0.75) = 1, and three copies contribute 3. For flew, 1 − p cancels in the same way, leaving (−2.25) × (−1/0.25) = 9. The result is 3 at every p, the exact slope of 3p − 1. Compare step 4: the same terms without the ratio gave 3.52 at p = 0.80. The ratio is exactly what removes the bias of the stored proportions.

At p = 0.90, what weights restore the current proportions, and what gain does the surrogate predict?

The weights are 0.90/0.75 = 1.2 for sat and 0.10/0.25 = 0.4 for flew. The weighted counts are 3.6 and 0.4, the proportions 9 : 1 of the current policy. The predicted gain is 3(0.90) − 2.25 = 0.45, which is 1.70 − 1.25.

Does this reweighting work for any policy and any response?

The probability ratio

It does. The cat-batch weights are an instance of importance weighting. An expectation under one distribution can be computed from samples of another by weighting each sample with the ratio of the two probabilities:

𝔼o∼πθ[f(o)]=𝔼o∼πold[πθ(o|x)πold(o|x)f(o)]

This holds when πold gives positive probability wherever πθ does. Sutton and Barto (§5.5, Eq. 5.3) call πold the behaviour policy and the weight the importance-sampling ratio.

PPO applies the ratio token by token. The state is the prompt with the generated prefix, and the sampled action is the next response token:

st=(x,o<t),ρt(θ)=πθ(ot|st)πold(ot|st)

A ratio of 1.2 means that the sampled token is now 20% more probable at that prefix; 0.8 means 20% less. In the cat batch only the first token is stochastic, so the token ratios are the weights p/0.75 and (1 − p)/0.25 used above. Multiplying each ratio by a fixed advantage estimate Ât gives the ratio surrogate (Lambert, Ch. 6):

Lratio(θ)=𝔼^t[ρt(θ)A^t]

Here 𝔼̂t follows the ML01 convention: average over the N responses, sum over the tokens of each response, so Lratio = (1/N) ∑i ∑t ρi,t Âi,t. In the cat batch the . and EOS tokens have ratio 1, so their terms add 2 × (mean advantage) = 0, and the batch value is 3p − 2.25. The surrogate predicts the gain in expected reward over πold, with the batch's rewards held fixed. In ML01 every token of response i carries the same advantage, Ai. The supplementary section below describes per-token advantages.

Step 7 used the general identity for the gradient of a ratio:

∇θρt=ρt∇θln⁡πθ(ot|st),ρt=1⇒∇θρt=∇θln⁡πθ(ot|st)

At the start of each optimisation stage, πθ = πold, every ratio is 1, and the surrogate gradient equals the REINFORCE gradient of ML01. Later steps reweight it.

The cat surrogate 3p − 2.25 keeps rising up to p = 1. Can it be trusted that far?

No. Even here it tracks the expected reward with the batch's rewards held fixed; the KL penalty grows as p moves, so at p = 0.90 the regularised gain is 0.31 against the surrogate's 0.45. In a real response, the later tokens also follow prefixes generated by πold. The token ratios correct the sampled token at each prefix. They do not correct which prefixes were visited. The surrogate is accurate only while πθ stays close to πold.

How can the surrogate stop rewarding changes that move the policy far from the batch?

The clipped surrogate

PPO compares the ratio-weighted advantage with a version whose ratio is clipped to [1 − ε, 1 + ε], and keeps the smaller of the two (Lambert, Ch. 6; Schulman et al., Eq. 7):

LCLIP(θ)=𝔼^t[min(ρtA^t,clip(ρt,1−ε,1+ε)A^t)]

A common choice is ε = 0.2. The advantage estimates stay fixed, and 𝔼̂t averages over responses and sums over tokens, as in Lratio. We maximise LCLIP, or minimise its negative.

  • For a positive advantage, raising the ratio beyond 1 + ε gives no further gain.
  • For a negative advantage, lowering the ratio below 1 − ε gives no further gain.
  • Changes in the harmful direction still lower the term. The minimum keeps the full penalty for them.

Clipping changes incentives in the sampled objective. It does not force every ratio into the interval, it does not bound the KL divergence, and it does not guarantee that the true objective improves.

What does clipping do to the cat batch?

Clipping in the cat batch

Use the batch sat, sat, sat, flew with advantages 0.75 and −2.25, and ε = 0.2.

Four fixed samples; batch mean of the surrogate term
Current pρ for satρ for flewUnclipped meanClipped mean
0.751.00001.00000.0000.000
0.801.06670.80000.1500.150
0.901.20000.40000.4500.225
0.951.26670.20000.6000.225

At p = 0.90, the sat term is min(1.2 × 0.75, 1.2 × 0.75) = 0.9. The flew term is min(0.4 × (−2.25), 0.8 × (−2.25)) = −1.8. The batch mean is (3 × 0.9 − 1.8)/4 = 0.225.

Beyond p = 0.80 the flew term is held at −1.8. Between 0.80 and 0.90 only the sat term still moves, so the slope of the clipped mean falls from 3 to 0.75. Beyond p = 0.90 the sat term is also held, at 0.9, and the clipped surrogate is flat: the sampled objective gives no reason to move further on this batch.

Clipping removes the incentive to move further. It does not stop the policy from moving. Past the limit in the favoured direction, a term is flat: its gradient is zero, so there is no push further and no push back. Ratios can still leave the interval. A step taken at p = 0.88, where the clipped slope is still 0.75, can overshoot to 0.95; there the ratios are 1.2667 and 0.2, both outside [0.8, 1.2], and the clipped mean is still 0.225. In a real model, one set of weights produces every token, so an update aimed at other tokens can also move a token whose own term is already flat, and optimisers with momentum keep moving after the gradient reaches zero. In the harmful direction, the minimum keeps the full penalty, and the gradient pulls the ratio back.

Why is the clipped flew term −1.8 and not −0.9?

The objective keeps the smaller value. For a negative advantage, clipping a ratio of 0.4 up to 0.8 makes the product more negative: 0.8 × (−2.25) = −1.8. Lowering the probability of flew below 0.8 of its rollout value therefore earns nothing more.

Is PPO clipping the same as gradient clipping in recurrent networks?

No. Both stabilise training. Gradient-norm clipping rescales the computed gradient so that its norm does not exceed a limit; it keeps the direction and does not set a nonzero gradient to zero. PPO clipping changes the objective before differentiation: past the limit, in the favoured direction, a sampled term is flat and its gradient is zero. Inside the interval PPO leaves the gradient unchanged, harmful moves keep the full penalty, and the limit is measured from πold across all the steps on one batch. In the cat batch, between p = 0.80 and 0.90 the flew term contributes zero gradient and the sat term contributes in full. The two can be used together.

How does this update fit into the RLHF loop of ML01?

PPO inside the RLHF loop

The ML01 loop changes in its update step. Generation, scoring and the KL-adjusted reward stay as they were.

  1. Collect a rollout batch. Set πold ← πθ. Generate responses with πold and store their token log-probabilities.
  2. Score and form advantages. Compute ri with the frozen reward model and ℓi with the frozen reference, then Ri = ri − β ℓi and the advantages. Hold them fixed for this batch.
  3. Optimise on the batch. Take a few gradient steps on minibatches of the stored responses, often one to four per batch. At each step maximise the clipped surrogate LCLIP, with ρt computed against the stored πold log-probabilities. Fit the baseline or value model on the same batch.
  4. Refresh and repeat. Collect a fresh batch with the updated policy. Keep πref fixed.

One round of generation and scoring now supports many gradient steps. In the ratio, πold measures change since the batch was collected. In the KL penalty, πref measures change since SFT. Replacing one with the other changes the method.

J&M §8.4.2 describes four model roles in a common PPO-based RLHF setup: the policy, the reference, the reward model and a value model. These roles need not use four separate networks. The value model supplies per-token advantages, described in the supplementary section.

PPO still needs a separate reward model and fresh generation for every batch. Can preference pairs train the generator directly?

Quick questions · 9 MCQs and 3 MSQs

An MSQ is correct only when you select all correct options and no extras. Scores are for self-checking. You can revisit a question and change your selection. Questions 1–9 follow the cat-batch calculations step by step; keep a pen and paper at hand.

Self-study questions
  1. Show that 𝔼o∼πold[(πθ/πold) f(o)] = 𝔼o∼πθ[f(o)]. What must hold for responses that πold never generates?
  2. Compute the ML01-loss gradient estimate on the stored cat batch at p = 0.70, term by term. Compare it with the exact slope 3, and then compute the reweighted gradient at the same p.
  3. Compute the clipped batch mean at p = 0.70. Why does clipping not change it?
  4. Repeat the cat-batch clipping table with ε = 0.1. Where does the clipped surrogate become flat?
  5. What goes wrong if PPO uses πref in the ratio denominator in place of πold?
  6. Why does the token ratio not correct for the prefixes that πold visited? Construct a two-token example in which this matters.

Supplementary: per-token advantages and the value model

Optional reading. Not required for ML03.

With one advantage per response, every token's log-probability gradient receives the same advantage weight. A learned value model V̂(st) estimates the expected remaining adjusted return from each prefix, as the critic did in the Block 4 actor–critic supplement. The token-level signal δt = rt + V̂(st+1) − V̂(st) provides a one-step advantage estimate for each token (with discount factor 1 and terminal value 0). Generalised advantage estimation combines these signals over several steps, in the spirit of the λ-returns of Sutton and Barto, Ch. 12. Lambert (Ch. 6) explains this extension. In RLHF implementations the reward model's score usually arrives at EOS, and the KL penalty is often charged token by token as part of rt.

The ratio and clipping mechanism is the same whichever advantage estimate is used. This microlecture uses the response-level advantages of ML01.

Microlecture 3

Direct preference optimisation

Instructor: Video · Slides (PDF)

AI version: Video · Slides (PDF)

Primary source: J&M §8.4.2, Eqs. 8.7–8.13, the two unnumbered DPO losses and Fig. 8.12. Textbook supplement: Lambert (2026), Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, Ch. 8. Rafailov et al. (2023) is the original DPO paper.

Training the generator on preference pairs

ML01 and ML02 trained the generator to maximise the KL-regularised objective of J&M Eq. 8.7:

π*=argmaxπ𝔼x∼D,o∼π(o|x)[rϕ(x,o)−βln⁡π(o|x)πref(o|x)]

PPO seeks to maximise this objective by sampling batches, scoring them with the reward model, and taking several gradient steps per batch. It does not guarantee a global maximum. Direct preference optimisation, DPO, trains the generator on the preference pairs themselves. Three problems stand between the objective and a loss on pairs.

Problems and solutions in this microlecture
ProblemSolution
A common PPO-based RLHF loop scores fresh rollout batches with a reward model and trains a value model, which adds computation.Closed-form optimum
The closed-form optimum depends on the reward, which is the model we want to remove.Invert for the reward
The inverted reward contains a sum over all possible responses, so it cannot be computed.Compare two responses

Which models does PPO keep during training?

Four model roles in PPO-based RLHF

A common PPO-based RLHF implementation has four model roles. The baseline here depends only on the prompt; a full critic can instead estimate return from each prefix.

Model roles in a common PPO-based RLHF setup
ModelRoleStatus
πθ, policyGenerates the responses. Updated by the clipped surrogate LCLIP.Trained
πref, referenceScores the sampled tokens for the log-ratio ℓ in the KL penalty.Frozen
rϕ, reward modelScores each complete response.Frozen
bψ, baseline (value model)Estimates the expected adjusted reward and forms the advantages.Trained

πold can be represented by the stored token log-probabilities for the batch. The policy and baseline need gradient updates; the reference and reward scorer stay fixed. Implementations can share parameters, so these roles do not require four separate networks. DPO uses a trainable policy and a frozen reference. Its reference scores can be cached before optimisation.

What policy maximises the KL-regularised objective for a fixed reward?

The closed-form optimum

An ideal optimum over response distributions has a closed-form expression. It ties the reward to policy probabilities, which is the relation DPO uses. Computing that expression for an LLM would still require an intractable normalisation sum.

Fix one prompt and drop x from the notation. Allow π to be any response distribution supported by πref, and assume the normalising sum is finite. A parameterised LLM may only approximate the optimum. For fixed reward r and β > 0, the objective is:

J(π)=∑oπ(o)[r(o)−βln⁡π(o)πref(o)]

Write the reward as a logarithm, r(o) = β ln er(o)/β, and combine the two logarithms:

=−β∑oπ(o)ln⁡π(o)πref(o)er(o)/β

The denominator πref(o)er(o)/β is not a probability distribution, because it need not sum to one. Divide it by its sum Z to obtain one, π*(o) = πref(o)er(o)/β/Z. Substituting πref(o)er(o)/β = Z π*(o) splits off ln Z, which is multiplied by ∑o π(o) = 1:

=−β∑oπ(o)ln⁡π(o)π*(o)+βln⁡Z

The remaining sum is the KL divergence from π to π*:

=βln⁡Z−βDKL(π∥π*)

β ln Z does not depend on π. The KL divergence is never negative and is zero only when π = π*. So π* is the maximiser, and the maximum value is β ln Z. Restoring the prompt:

π*(o|x)=πref(o|x)er(x,o)/βZ(x),Z(x)=∑oπref(o|x)er(x,o)/β

Each response keeps its reference probability, multiplied by er/β. Higher-reward responses receive larger factors. Z(x) is the partition function: it normalises the result so that the probabilities sum to one.

The cat example, β = 2

Reference 0.75 for sat . EOS and 0.25 for flew . EOS; rewards 2 and −1.

Closed-form optimum for “The cat”
FactorValueWhere it comes from
0.75 × e2/22.038711Reference probability of sat times its factor e1 = 2.718
0.25 × e−1/20.151633Reference probability of flew times its factor e−0.5 = 0.607
Z2.190344Sum of the two numerators
π*(sat)0.9310.75e/2.190344… ≈ 0.930772
π*(flew)0.0690.25e−0.5/2.190344… ≈ 0.069228
β ln Z1.5682 ln(2.190344…) ≈ 1.568117, the maximum value of the objective

Values in this table are rounded. Calculations use the unrounded exponentials and normaliser.

ML01 located the same maximum numerically, by plotting the regularised objective against p: the maximum was at p = 0.931 with value 1.568. The closed form gives both numbers directly.

Repeat the calculation with β = 1 and with β = 5. What happens to π*(sat)?

With β = 1: Z = 0.75e2 + 0.25e−1 = 5.542 + 0.092 = 5.634, so π*(sat) = 0.984. With β = 5: Z = 0.75e0.4 + 0.25e−0.2 = 1.119 + 0.205 = 1.324, so π*(sat) = 0.845. A smaller β lets the reward move the policy further from the reference.

The optimum needs the reward. Can we read this relation backwards, to express the reward through the policy?

The reward from the optimal policy

DPO aims to remove the reward model. The closed form links each reward to the probabilities of π* and πref, so solve it for r. Take logarithms:

ln⁡π*(o|x)=ln⁡πref(o|x)+r(x,o)β−ln⁡Z(x)

Multiply by β and rearrange:

r(x,o)=βln⁡π*(o|x)πref(o|x)+βln⁡Z(x)

This is J&M Eq. 8.10, written with π* for the optimal policy. A reward is β times the log-ratio of the optimal policy to the reference, plus a term that depends only on the prompt.

Recovering the cat rewards

The log-ratio terms need only π* and πref:

sat: 2 ln(0.9307722…/0.75) ≈ 0.432.
flew: 2 ln(0.0692278…/0.25) ≈ −2.568.

Adding β ln Z ≈ 1.568 gives the rewards: approximately 0.432 + 1.568 = 2 and −2.568 + 1.568 = −1. The unrounded values recover 2 and −1 exactly.

The value Z ≈ 2.190344 came from the closed form, which used the rewards 2 and −1. The two log-ratio terms do not need Z.

Without the rewards, Z(x) is unknown. It sums over every possible response to the prompt: for an LLM with a 50,000-token vocabulary and 20-token responses, 50,00020 ≈ 1094 terms. So Eq. 8.10 cannot give the reward of a single response.

Preferences compare two responses to the same prompt. What happens to β ln Z(x) in that comparison?

The partition function cancels

The reward model was trained with the Bradley–Terry model (J&M Eqs. 8.8–8.9). For a prompt x with preferred response ow and dispreferred response ol, it uses only the reward difference:

P(ow≻ol|x)=σ(r(x,ow)−r(x,ol))

Substitute Eq. 8.10 for both rewards. Both responses answer the same prompt, so both carry the same β ln Z(x), and the two terms cancel in the difference:

P(ow≻ol|x)=σ(βln⁡π*(ow|x)πref(ow|x)−βln⁡π*(ol|x)πref(ol|x))

This is J&M Eqs. 8.12–8.13. Only the two compared responses are needed, and Z(x) is never computed. J&M write πθ in Eq. 8.13; at this point of the derivation the policy is π*, and πθ enters in the next step.

The cat comparison, β = 2

sat ≻ flew: 0.432 − (−2.568) = 3. The 1.568 terms cancel, and 3 is the reward gap 2 − (−1).

The predicted preference probability is σ(3) = 1/(1 + e−3) = 0.953.

Why must the two responses answer the same prompt?

Z(x) depends on the prompt. For two different prompts the terms β ln Z(x1) and β ln Z(x2) differ and do not cancel, so the difference would again need a sum over all responses.

π* is unknown. Can a trainable policy πθ take its place and be fitted to the preference labels?

The DPO loss

Replace π* with the trainable πθ. The argument of σ becomes the margin:

mθ=βln⁡πθ(ow|x)πref(ow|x)−βln⁡πθ(ol|x)πref(ol|x)

σ(mθ) is the predicted probability of the recorded preference. Fit the preference labels by maximum likelihood, that is, by minimising the cross-entropy loss (J&M §8.4.2, the two unnumbered DPO losses):

LDPO(x,ow,ol)=−ln⁡σ(mθ),LDPO(πθ)=−𝔼(x,ow,ol)∼D[ln⁡σ(mθ)]

Each response log-probability ln π(o | x) is the sum of its token log-probabilities, including EOS. Prompt and padding tokens are excluded from this sum. The loss favours increasing the preferred-versus-rejected margin relative to the reference. With shared model parameters, this does not guarantee that one response probability rises and the other falls. J&M give typical values of β from 0.01 to 0.1. The cat example uses β = 2 so that the numbers stay readable.

The cat example: one label sat ≻ flew, β = 2

With p = πθ(sat . EOS | x) and reference 0.75 and 0.25, the margin is

mθ = 2[ln(p/0.75) − ln((1 − p)/0.25)] = 2[ln(p/(1 − p)) − ln 3].

Factors of the cat margin
FactorWhere it comes from
2β
ln(p/0.75)Log-ratio of sat, the preferred response
ln((1 − p)/0.25)Log-ratio of flew, the dispreferred response
ln(p/(1 − p))Log-odds of sat under πθ
ln 3Log-odds of sat under πref, 0.75/0.25 = 3
DPO loss for one label, β = 2
pOdds of satMargin mθσ(mθ)Loss −ln σ
0.601.52 ln 0.5 = −1.3860.21.609
0.75300.50.693
0.9092 ln 3 = 2.1970.90.105

At p = 0.75, πθ equals πref, both log-ratios are zero, and the prediction is 0.5. At p = 0.60, sat is still the more probable response, but its odds have fallen from the reference's 3 to 1.5, so the margin is negative and the loss is large.

At p = 0.80, is σ(mθ) the probability that πθ generates sat?

No. The odds are 4, so mθ = 2 ln(4/3) = 0.575 and σ(mθ) = 0.64, while πθ generates sat with probability 0.80. σ(mθ) predicts the preference label. At p = 0.90 the two numbers happen to coincide, both 0.9.

What the labels decide

With the single label sat ≻ flew, the loss keeps falling as p grows: 0.048 at p = 0.931 and 0.0009 at p = 0.99. It approaches zero as p → 1. Nothing in the loss stops at π*(sat) = 0.931.

The closed form describes a different situation: labels that follow Bradley–Terry. Suppose a fraction q of the labels for this pair prefer sat. The expected loss per pair and its derivative in the margin are:

−[qln⁡σ(m)+(1−q)ln⁡σ(−m)],ddm=σ(m)−q

The derivative is zero where σ(m) = q. If the labels come from the reward gap 3, then q = σ(3) = 0.953, the minimum is at m = 3, and 2[ln(p/(1 − p)) − ln 3] = 3 gives p = 0.931 = π*(sat). Thus DPO recovers the KL-regularised optimum in this two-response population example. More generally, this connection requires Bradley–Terry-consistent preferences, enough comparison coverage, a policy that can represent the optimum and ideal optimisation.

Three of every four labels prefer sat. Where is the DPO minimum?

σ(m) = 0.75 gives m = ln 3. Then 2[ln(p/(1 − p)) − ln 3] = ln 3, so the odds are 3e(ln 3)/2 = 3√3 = 5.196 and p = 0.839.

The reference probabilities and β enter every DPO margin. They define the reward–policy relation, but the finite-data loss does not enforce a fixed KL budget. With sparse or consistently one-sided preference labels, optimisation can suppress rejected responses and move away from the reference. Monitor both preference performance and policy drift.

What does a DPO training run need, and how do the pieces fit together?

DPO training

DPO is gradient descent on the DPO loss over a fixed set of preference pairs D.

  1. Initialise. Copy πθ and πref from πSFT. Freeze πref. Choose β.
  2. Score the pairs with the reference. For each pair (x, ow, ol) in D, compute ln πref(ow | x) and ln πref(ol | x) once. πref is frozen, so these values never change.
  3. Score a minibatch with the policy. Compute ln πθ(ow | x), ln πθ(ol | x) and the margin mθ.
  4. Update. Take a gradient step on the mean of −ln σ(mθ). Repeat over D.

J&M list three advantages of DPO over PPO.

Advantages of DPO over PPO (J&M §8.4.2)
AdvantageWhy
No reward modelThe preferences train πθ directly. rϕ is never fitted.
No online samplingD is fixed. πθ generates no responses during training.
Two models, not fourπθ is trained and πref is frozen. There is no rϕ and no bψ.

DPO is cheaper and simpler. Why do current training pipelines still use PPO-style reinforcement learning?

DPO or PPO?

The main difference is how training obtains feedback.

Standard offline DPO and PPO-based RLHF
AspectStandard offline DPOPPO-based RLHF
Training responsesUses a fixed set of labelled preference pairs. Online or iterative variants collect new pairs.Collects fresh current-policy rollout batches and scores those responses.
Reward evidenceFits an implicit reward through the policy and reference log-ratios.Fits a separate reward model, then queries it during policy training.
GeneralisationCan score unseen responses through the learned log-ratios. Its accuracy depends on the training evidence.A learned reward model can also score unseen responses. Its accuracy depends on the training evidence.
Reference and regularisationThe reference and β enter every preference margin. Finite-data training gives no hard KL budget.The reference defines an explicit KL penalty, estimated on sampled responses. This is a soft penalty; clipping also gives no hard KL bound.

Preference labels can come from human judges, AI judges or automatic checks. A checker for a known mathematics answer or code tests can score each generated response directly. Using such scores as rewards for reinforcement learning is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, RLVR (J&M Ch. 8 introduction). The same scores can also form preference pairs for DPO, for example a passing response preferred to a failing response. Direct reward optimisation and training on derived pairs use the feedback in different ways.

Can an automatic checker score the policy’s generated responses directly?

Quick questions · 9 MCQs and 3 MSQs

Self-study questions
  1. Verify the derivation of the closed form for a prompt with three responses, reference 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2, rewards 1, 0 and −1, and β = 1. Check that J(π*) = β ln Z.
  2. For the same three responses, recover each reward from π* and πref with Eq. 8.10.
  3. Show that adding a constant c(x) to every reward for a prompt leaves π* unchanged. What happens to Z(x)?
  4. Compute the cat margin, σ(mθ) and the loss at p = 0.70 with β = 2. Repeat with β = 0.1.
  5. With β = 2, differentiate −ln σ(mθ) with respect to p in the cat example. Why does the gradient magnitude shrink as p → 1?
  6. A data set has 60 labels sat ≻ flew and 40 labels flew ≻ sat. Where is the DPO minimum for β = 2?

Objectives, procedures and evidence

What the two training procedures use
AspectRLHF using PPOStandard offline DPO
Preference pairsFit the reward scorerTrain the generator directly

KL regularisation specifies a reward–departure tradeoff. PPO is a sampled policy-optimisation procedure. DPO turns a reward–policy relationship into a loss on labelled preference pairs. Improved training loss still needs evaluation against the intended task.

Discussion questions
  1. Explain why a response-independent baseline and a reference-policy penalty have different effects on the objective.
  2. What can go wrong if PPO uses the SFT reference in place of the rollout-policy denominator?
  3. Why does clipping behave differently for positive and negative advantages?
  4. Why does DPO need both responses to answer the same prompt for the normaliser to cancel?
  5. Why can better preference prediction still fail to improve factual accuracy?
